title: About 70% of vendor bills above PO value are paid in full: $314,943.32 a year paid above PO, spread evenly across vendors and every other recorded attribute. It is not shown to be a loss, and no recorded rule explains which bills get short-paid
conclusion: Observed, 2016-2025, excluding duplicate '-R' re-bills. 20,121 bills have line value above PO value. Of these, 13,901 were paid in full, carrying $3,149,433.24 above PO; 5,911 were short-paid exactly to PO value; 309 are unpaid (q222). That is $314,943.32 a year (q234). It is a steady level, not a spike: $423,467.54 in 2016, then $270,039.09-$332,254.38 a year in 2017-2025, with a 2023-2025 average of $308,642.46 and an average excluding 2016 of $302,885.08 (q209, q219). The excess splits into $2,317,669.52 of extra quantity valued at PO cost and $831,763.72 of unit cost above PO (q222). The share of bills above PO is flat across all 44 vendors (4.54%-6.18%), and so is the share paid in full (62.4%-77.1%) (q138). OEM vendors 1-4 carry most of the dollars because their units cost more (q168). They do not bill above PO more often. Among paid over-PO bills, the full-pay rate is 0.702 overall (q234). It stays near that level by year, type and terms (q157), and by branch, month, vendor kind, absolute excess, bill size and the previous bill's outcome (q201, q213). Excesses of $1,000 or more are paid in full at 0.691, against 0.703 for excesses under $50 (q201). The extra quantity on stock lines that was paid in full comes to $839,490.41, or $83,949.04 a year (q219, q234). For those lines, WMS records receipt of the PO quantity. But WMS receipts equal the PO quantity on all 470,300 received stock lines (q194), so that record is weak evidence that the extra units were not delivered. Freight is not shown to be excess. No vendor credit matches any overbill (q191). Interpretation: the payments above PO are real in the records. Nothing in the data explains why some over-PO bills are short-paid and others are not. That could be an AP practice, information that was never recorded, or the way the records were produced, and this data cannot tell them apart. Action: ask AP whether a bill-vs-PO match exists and how exceptions are released. Before claiming credits on stock-quantity overbills, ask vendors for proof of delivery.

claims.text: Excluding '-R' bills, 20,121 bills have line value above PO value. 13,901 were paid in full ($3,149,433.24 excess), 5,911 were short-paid to PO value ($1,371,706.45) and 309 are unpaid ($63,588.14). All 335,559 matched bills that were paid were paid in full. 6,115 bills whose lines match the PO were short-paid by exactly their freight. The join is sound: every bill amount equals lines plus freight, with 0 duplicate SKUs, 0 multi-payment bills, 0 bill lines off the PO and 0 unbilled lines on billed POs.

Paid-in-full excess is $314,943.32 a year over 2016-2025. By year it was $423,467.54 in 2016 and $270,039.09-$332,254.38 in 2017-2025. The 2023-2025 average is $308,642.46 and the average excluding 2016 is $302,885.08.

Of the $3,149,433.24 paid-in-full excess, $2,317,669.52 is extra quantity at PO cost and $831,763.72 ($83,176.37 a year) is unit cost above PO. The unit-cost part cannot be judged without contract prices. Above-PO costs fall at 1.03x-1.08x the PO cost and do not persist: the next bill for the same SKU is above PO 2.88% of the time against a 2.49% base rate.

Billing above PO is not concentrated by vendor. All 44 vendors have 4.54%-6.18% of bills above PO and pay 62.4%-77.1% of those in full. OEMs (vendors 1-4) hold 80.58% of the excess against 55.47% of PO value. Their average unit cost is $1,183.94, against $92.69 for parts and $106.65 for supplies.

The full-pay rate among paid over-PO bills is 0.702 (13,901 of 19,812). By branch it ranges 0.683-0.723 (n 1,492-1,774), by month 0.681-0.723 and by vendor kind 0.696-0.705. Excesses under $50 are paid in full at 0.703 (n=8,428) and excesses of $1,000 or more at 0.691 (n=1,601). Bills of $25k or more are paid in full at 0.717 (n=336). After a full-paid over-PO bill from the same vendor, the next one is full-paid at 0.698; after a short-paid one, at 0.711. By year the rate is 0.687-0.724, and across terms 0.684-0.712.

Stock-line extra quantity paid in full is $839,490.41, or $83,949.04 a year (2023-2025 average $81,673.99). On all 3,631 such lines WMS records receipt of the PO quantity. But receipts equal the PO quantity on all 470,300 received stock lines, with 0 short, 0 over and 0 split receipts. Bills are never below the PO: 0 of 595,478 lines are under in quantity or cost. Special-order lines have no receipts at all.

Freight paid on full-paid bills was $2,076,290.17 over 10 years. Of this, $1,956,020.09 is on bills whose lines match the PO exactly and $120,270.08 on over-PO bills. Bills carrying freight are paid in full at 0.700. Nothing shows the freight was not owed, so it is excluded from the size.

No recovery is visible. There are 1,234 vendor credits totalling $1,929,606.50. None of them has an amount equal to the billed excess on an over-quantity bill with the same vendor and SKU within 252 operating days.

not_evidence_of: Not evidence that any vendor overbills on purpose, or that anyone approving payments did anything wrong. It does not show the paid excess is a loss: unit costs or freight may be contractually owed, extra units may have been delivered but receipted only up to the PO quantity, and recoveries may exist outside these records. It is not evidence of a vendor-specific problem; the OEM dollar share comes from unit price. Interpretation: the 70/30 split is equally uniform across every dimension tested, including the size of the excess. That fits a recording or data-generation artefact as well as it fits human AP decisions, so it is not evidence of an 'inconsistently applied match'.
could_not_tell: Whether higher unit costs or freight were contractually owed: there are no price agreements or freight terms. Whether extra units were delivered: WMS receipts mirror the PO quantity, and special orders are never received. Whether any excess was recovered: credits have no link to bills. Who or what decided to short-pay some bills: there is no approver or match-exception record. Needed: the AP match-exception log or approval workflow, vendor contracts and freight terms, proof-of-delivery documents, and a link from credits to bills.
next_step: Ask AP whether a three-way match exists, how its exceptions are released, and whether a log of them exists. For the stock-quantity overbills ($83,949.04 a year), ask vendors for proof of delivery before claiming credits, starting with recent years. Get contract prices for the $83,176.37 a year of unit-cost excess. Review the 1,429 '-R' duplicate bills ($4,196,810.04, q184) as a separate finding.
dead_ends: Vendor concentration in behaviour: the over-PO rate and full-pay rate are flat across all 44 vendors (q138)
Price-increase explanation: above-PO costs do not persist on later bills for the same SKU (q149)
Any rule for full-pay vs short-pay by year, type, purpose, excess size, freight or terms (q157), or by branch, month, kind, absolute excess, bill size or the previous outcome (q201, q213): none found
Join or definition artefacts: none found (q187, q188, q189)
Vendor credits as recovery of overbills: no amount matches (q191)
response_to_challenge: Accepted in full; no part needed a counter-query. (1) Mechanics: the challenger's checks confirm the '-R' exclusion and the join, and q222 reproduces my q130 figures exactly, so the counts and dollars stand. (2) Hidden rule: accepted. The full-pay rate is also flat by branch, month, kind, absolute excess, bill size and the previous outcome (q201, q213). I dropped 'inconsistently applied match' as the conclusion and now list it as one of several readings the data cannot separate. (3) WMS evidence: accepted. Receipts equal the PO quantity on all 470,300 received stock lines (q194), so 'contradicted by WMS' becomes 'WMS records only the PO quantity'. That supports a request for proof of delivery, not a credit claim. (4) Freight: accepted. $1,956,020.09 of the $2,076,290.17 is on matched bills (q222), so the $207,629.02 a year and the $522,572.34 combined figure are removed. (5) Recovery: accepted; no credit matches (q191). (6) Trend: accepted. I added the yearly range and the averages excluding 2016 and for 2023-2025 (q209, q219), so the reader can see that 2016 lifts the 10-year average. (7) Money: accepted. The headline stays $314,943.32 a year, now labelled 'paid above PO value' rather than loss, and is split into quantity and unit-cost parts (q222, q234). Small note: the stock-quantity figure ($839,490.41) values the extra units at billed unit cost (q209), while the quantity/cost split values them at PO cost (q222). So the two are not meant to be summed. Size query moved to q234, which contains 314943.32.
